subject: Architecture
title: Prefab Revolution: Factories Building Buildings
description: One-minute skill: Prefab Revolution: Factories Building Buildings.

hook.text: A Chinese company assembled a 57-story skyscraper in 19 days — every piece was built in a factory first.

buildup.text: Prefabricated modules are built indoors — with wiring, plumbing, and finishes — then trucked to the site.

discovery.text: Factory conditions mean better quality control, fewer weather delays, and 30% less construction waste.

twist.text: Sweden builds 90% of houses from prefab wood — 'BoKlok' by IKEA delivers flat-pack apartments.

climax.text: Singapore mandates prefab construction for public housing — every new block uses factory-made modules.

punchline.text: The building site of the future is a factory floor.

quiz.question: What country mandates prefab construction for public housing?

details.summary: Modern prefabrication manufactures entire building modules — walls, floors, bathrooms, kitchens — in factories and assembles them on-site in days. Factory conditions improve quality control, reduce waste by up to 80%, and slash construction schedules while insulating work from weather delays.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional construction is one of the least productive industries. Prefabrication brings manufacturing efficiency to building, producing higher quality at lower cost. It could transform how fast and affordably cities can grow.
takeaways: Factory-built modules are assembled on-site in days
Waste reduction reaches up to 80% compared to traditional methods
Factory conditions improve quality and eliminate weather delays

faq.question: Are prefab buildings lower quality than traditional?
faq.answer: The opposite is often true. Factory conditions enable precise quality control, consistent material handling, and inspection at every stage. Joints, finishes, and structural connections are typically more accurate than field-built equivalents.

faq.question: Why hasn't prefab construction taken over entirely?
faq.answer: Transportation limits module size, building codes vary by jurisdiction, and the construction industry resists change. Unions, local regulations, and the custom nature of most buildings create barriers. However, adoption is accelerating rapidly as housing shortages worsen globally.
